title: Claims & Argument Structure — Skill Check
description: Identify the main claim, supporting claims, and how the argument’s parts build on one another.
subject: rla
passage:
The student transportation committee recommends converting 12 of the campus’s 286 car-parking spaces into a covered, lockable bicycle area for a one-year trial. The committee’s main claim is that secure bicycle storage would solve a specific barrier for students who already want to ride to campus without causing a serious parking shortage.

Campus security recorded 18 bicycle theft reports last academic year. Fourteen involved bicycles left at the uncovered racks beside the east classroom buildings. In a transportation survey, 37 percent of students who said they would consider cycling more often identified theft or weather exposure as a major concern. The committee argues that a monitored, covered storage area directly addresses both concerns.

Some drivers object that removing any car spaces will make morning parking worse. The committee responds that parking counts taken on twelve typical weekdays showed at least 34 unused spaces even during the busiest thirty-minute arrival period. It proposes placing the bicycle area at the edge of the east lot, where those counts found the most consistent unused capacity.

Another student group suggests that the college should instead expand discounted bus passes. The committee supports that idea as a separate transportation option but argues that bus discounts do not answer the storage problem faced by students who already own bicycles. The proposal therefore asks for a limited trial, followed by theft reports, bicycle-use counts, and parking counts before any permanent change.

questions.prompt: What is the committee’s main claim?
questions.explanation: This choice best matches the argument: A small secure bicycle-storage trial could remove a cycling barrier without seriously reducing parking.
questions.rule: Track the exact claim, evidence, and reasoning before judging the argument.

options.text: All students should stop driving to campus.
options.whyWrong: The proposal is a limited bicycle-storage trial, not a ban on driving.

options.text: A small secure bicycle-storage trial could remove a cycling barrier without seriously reducing parking.
Bus passes are harmful to campus transportation.
options.whyWrong: The committee supports bus discounts as a separate option.

options.text: Every bicycle theft happened in the east lot.
options.whyWrong: Fourteen of eighteen reported thefts involved east-side racks, not all thefts.

options.text: The college should convert every parking space into bicycle storage.
Students who drive should receive free bus passes.
options.whyWrong: This is not the committee’s proposal.

options.text: The east lot has enough unused capacity to host the trial without creating a serious shortage.
The trial should last exactly one year because one year is always sufficient.
options.whyWrong: The one-year period is proposed, but this is not argued as a universal rule.

questions.prompt: Which statement is a supporting claim the committee uses to defend the bicycle-storage trial?
questions.explanation: This supporting claim connects the parking-count evidence to the committee’s larger claim that the trial can occur without a serious parking shortage.
questions.rule: A supporting claim helps carry the main claim and is backed by its own evidence.

options.text: Every student should travel by bicycle.
options.whyWrong: The committee proposes one transportation option and never claims everyone should cycle.

options.text: Bus discounts should be eliminated.
options.whyWrong: The committee supports bus discounts as a separate option.

The bicycle area must become permanent after one year.
